articles.text: During the May 8 Piedmont School Board meeting the board shined a spotlight on the progress of the racial equity board policy approved in September 2020. The racial equity policy, a piece of the larger educational equity policy, received a thorough review four years into the work in a city hall packed with enthusiastic supporters. Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen called the current moment in history ripe to assess the progress of the policy. Especially, “in the midst of hateful narratives that are calling for the end of [Diversity, Equity, Inclusive and Belonging] work,” she said. Jean Takazawa, in her first year as the Director of DEI at PUSD, spoke at length about progress made with the restorative justice circles. Takazawak reiterated that she is firm believer in restorative justice and thanked students for their work. Takazawa and Restorative Justice Consultant Ina Bendich spent time last year in Spring training 35 high school students to be community circle keepers. “It’s one thing to say it in practice, but then it’s another thing to actually be in the classroom and have 25 kids do a circle,” said Takazawa. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich also delineated vital information during the board presentation. “I want to take a moment to comment on what it means to adopt a curriculum with an anti-racist lens,” said Dolowich. “To be clear, there’s absolutely no intention to adopt a separate standalone curriculum. This is a lens in terms of how we review, pilot, and adopt curriculum moving forward.” Dolowich then specified what an anti-racist lens looks like for a teacher in the classroom and three things they are asked to do. “One, as educators, to have a level of self-awareness and training. Two, to understand our own biases and specifically, implicit, biases that we bring,” said Dolowich. Dolowich concluded with what he described as most critical and fundamental for students. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Jewish Community held an evening of visual and sensory experiences titled “Truth and Remembrance” at the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) on Wednesday, May 15. Titled an “evening of visual and musical creativity, remembrance and honor,” the art installation featured video presentations, photography exhibits, musical interludes and a candlelit memorial dedicated to the lives lost in the Israel-Hamas war. According to organizers, approximately 200 people attended the event which took place between 7:00 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. The greatest contribution of the evening was made by the 35-year-old Israeli singer-songwriter and music producer Orion Stone. “We need to focus on the living, not on revenge,” declared Stone. “Our grandparents fled the Holocaust to create a better future in Israel, not to plot their revenge.” Three of Stone’s family members were killed during the attacks on October 7, 2023. articles.text: Donors to receive T-shirts The American Red Cross will hold a blood drive in Piedmont at Veterans’ Memorial Hall (401 Highland Avenue) this Saturday, May 25 from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Additionally, the Red Cross has teamed up with the creators of the videogame Tetris to celebrate the game’s 40th anniversary. People who make blood or Power RED donations before June 9 will receive an exclusive Tetris + Red Cross T-shirt while supplies last. Donors will also automatically be entered for a chance to win a trip for two to New York to meet Tetris creator Alexey Pajitnov. According to the Red Cross, every two seconds someone in the U.S. needs blood or platelets, but only about 3% of age-eligible people donate each year. Blood donations through the Red Cross are used for patients in need of surgery, cancer treatment and transfusions for blood loss from traumatic injuries. In addition to traditional blood donation, the Red Cross will also be soliciting “Power Red” donations. In this new process, a specialized machine allows donors to safely donate two units of red blood cells during one donation while also returning any plasma and platelets to the donor’s body. This way, donors can give nearly twice the amount of red cells at one time and help more patients. Power Red donations are an effective method for busy donors looking to maximize their impact on the community. Power red cell donation takes about 20-30 minutes longer than a whole blood donation and you can donate approximately every four months. Donors may select either blood donation or Power Red donation at the time of registration. To register for an appointment, visit http://RedCrossBlood.org and enter sponsor code PIEDMONT, or call 1-800-REDCROSS. This is a city-sponsored event. articles.text: Mayor Jen Cavenaugh’s State of the City address on Tuesday, May 7, gathered both city officials and members of the public at the Community Hall for a recap of the year’s accomplishments and a glimpse at the projects the City currently has underway. “Tonight is about celebrating Piedmont, not just for what it has been, but for what we’re building here together,” said Cavenaugh. “You’re here because you care deeply for our city and its future, and that’s what we’re celebrating.” A State of the City address is a recent tradition, according to former Mayor Bob McBain. “It’s not a long-term tradition, but it’s an effort which I thought made a lot of sense,” said McBain, who served on the Piedmont City Council from 2012 to 2020 and as mayor from 2017 to 2020. “I suggested that people do it because it’s a useful tool that lets people know exactly what their city government’s been doing.” Former mayor Margaret Fujioka delivered her State of the City address in 2016. McBain planned on delivering his own speech but had to cancel it due to restrictions on in-person gatherings during the COVID-19 pandemic. Previous mayor Teddy King delivered her speech in 2022. During her presentation, Cavenaugh noted several milestones in the past year including the expansion of the public safety camera and Automated License Plate Reader programs by the police department, as well as the launch of multiple new digital services by the City, including tools for submitting online planning and building permits and the new real-time crime map implemented by the police via Citizen Connect. Cavenaugh addressed challenges facing Piedmont including regional issues like rising crime, housing costs, and the growing demands on Piedmont including the City’s aging infrastructure. “We possess all the necessary ingredients – the vision, the leadership, and most important, the partnership with … our incredible residents to not only overcome these hurdles but to thrive,” she said. “I think that what came across was how much she has appreciated being in Piedmont, and appreciated the opportunity to serve the community,” said McBain. Mayor Cavenaugh delivers her speech in Piedmont Community Hall.

articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery will celebrate its 100th annual Memorial Day service at 10:00 a.m. this Monday, May 27, in a ceremony which welcomes the public. It will include guest speakers from the Armed Forces, a salute to fallen and music tributes. The event will take place in front of the Veterans’ Memorial Stone on the main drive. Refreshments – including donuts, hot dogs, and coffee – will be served before and after the service. This is a free event, and no tickets are required for entry. “It’s a time where we gather the community and remind everyone, all our community members and veterans, about how much we appreciate the sacrifices of our servicemen and servicewomen throughout for their sacrifice,” said Kristie Ly, the event organizer at Mountain View Cemetery. “Even if we don’t know them, we must be grateful for their sacrifices. They risked their lives so we can live ours.” Every year, people from all over the Bay Area attend Mountain View Cemetery’s Memorial Day ceremony because of the loved ones they have buried there. The ceremony includes an appearance by Piedmont Highlanders Drums and Pipes, Piedmont’s bagpipe band, and Piedmont Scout Troop 6 as color guard, which will conduct a flag ceremony. Singing group Tosca will perform patriotic songs, and brass musicians with The Hardiman Trio will play taps. This year’s guest speaker will be Lt. Col. Bradlee Seehawer, an active-duty airman stationed at Travis Air Force Base. The Master Florists Association has donated long-stem roses for audience members to lay on their loved mone’s graves. articles.text: Have you ever wondered what skills you need to work with animals at the Zoo? Zookeepers and veterinarians are skilled in making careful observations. An observation is when we gather information through our senses, such as seeing, hearing, or smelling. Making observations is an important part of being a scientist. The animals who live at the Zoo can’t talk, so zookeepers and veterinarians carefully observe the animals’ behavior to ensure their happiness and health. When we observe animals engaging with fun things in their habitat, eating, and resting, we can tell they are healthy and comfortable. If we observe animals sleeping more than usual, not eating their food, or limping, we know they may need help. Zookeepers and veterinarians are scientists because they write down their observations. This allows them to learn how animal behavior changes over time, and detailed observations help us make the best decisions about what the animals need and want. Activity You can make observations like a zoo scientist, too. You’ll need a timer, a piece of paper, a pencil, and one animal to observe. This animal could be a pet in your home, a lizard in your yard, or a squirrel at a park. If you can’t find an animal, you can also watch live videos of animals at the Oakland Zoo (oaklandzoo. org/webcams). Pick one animal to watch, set a timer for 10 minutes and write down every behavior you observe (zoo scientists call this continuous sampling). Try to write down at least one behavior each minute, even if it’s the same behavior twice. You can also draw a picture. After 10 minutes review your notes. What did the animal do the most? What did they do the least? Do you notice any patterns? Congratulations! You’re now an animal behavior scientist! Do you have a burning question for an animal expert? Submit questions to education@ oaklandzoo.org with “Piedmont Post” as the subject for a chance to be featured in Oakland Zoo’s final article this year. Wilson Sherman is Program Manager of Community Engagement at Oakland Zoo. Photo by Wilson Sherman Oakland Zoo summer campers make observations at the Hamadryas baboon exhibit.

DON’T MISS OUT— REGISTER TODAY! www.piedmontadultschool.org 510-594-2655 Thinking Outside the Classroom Observe animal behavior like a zoo scientist By Wilson Sherman Have you ever wondered what skills you need to work with animals at the Zoo? Zookeepers and veterinarians are skilled in making careful observations. An observation is when we gather information through our senses, such as seeing, hearing, or smelling. Making observations is an important part of being a scientist. The animals who live at the Zoo can’t talk, so zookeepers and veterinarians carefully observe the animals’ behavior to ensure their happiness and health. When we observe animals engaging with fun things in their habitat, eating, and resting, we can tell they are healthy and comfortable. If we observe animals sleeping more than usual, not eating their food, or limping, we know they may need help. Zookeepers and veterinarians are scientists because they write down their observations. This allows them to learn how animal behavior changes over time, and detailed observations help us make the best decisions about what the animals need and want. Activity You can make observations like a zoo scientist, too. You’ll need a timer, a piece of paper, a pencil, and one animal to observe. This animal could be a pet in your home, a lizard in your yard, or a squirrel at a park. If you can’t find an animal, you can also watch live videos of animals at the Oakland Zoo (oaklandzoo. org/webcams). Pick one animal to watch, set a timer for 10 minutes and write down every behavior you observe (zoo scientists call this continuous sampling). Try to write down at least one behavior each minute, even if it’s the same behavior twice. You can also draw a picture. After 10 minutes review your notes. What did the animal do the most? What did they do the least? Do you notice any patterns? Congratulations! You’re now an animal behavior scientist! Do you have a burning question for an animal expert? Submit questions to education@ oaklandzoo.org with “Piedmont Post” as the subject for a chance to be featured in Oakland Zoo’s final article this year. articles.text: Ukranian Vlad Putrenkov now delivering for the neighborhood Piedmont Post paperboy Vlad Putrenkov delivers papers for the neighborhoods of Requa, Highland and Wildwood. Ever y Wednesday after school, third-grader Vlad Putrenkov walks to the Piedmont Center for the Arts to pick up a stack of papers and tucks them into his canvas delivery bag. After folding his supply of papers, he delivers the Piedmont Post to subscribers on his route, which includes Highland, Requa and Wildwood Avenue. “The hardest part is carrying the bag,” said Putrenkov. “It gets to be around 15 pounds, once a month for the All-City edition.” After nearly three months on the job, Putrenkov can now land his papers squarely at front doors with startling accuracy. “It’s just like baseball,” he said. And Vlad loves baseball. Vlad began delivering in February 2024 when he was put in touch with the Piedmont Post by his mother’s friend, Mary Ann Parachini, who thought it would be a good way for him to meet members of the community. The son of Ukrainian immigrants Alexander Putrenkov and Maryna Putrenkova, Vlad and his family came to the United States in April 2022 following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian War just two months earlier. “It was scary,” recalled Maryna. “They were shooting. The city immediately closed schools, hospitals, and grocery stores were left without food. There were armed soldiers and tanks on the streets. The police ceased to exist, and thefts became more frequent. People were kidnapped.” Since moving to Piedmont with the help of a sponsorship from Piedmont Community Church, the Putrenkov family has adjusted well to the town. Maryna said the greatest surprise was the kindness of the community. “The Miller family took us in for a while and helped get Vlad into Wildwood School. They also introduced us to the church in Piedmont where we made many friends. We are very grateful to the Miller family and our church members for helping us adapt to this country at such a difficult time for us.” She also thanked Piedmont resident Mary Ann Parachini for allowing her family to stay at her house for a short period. “We are also very grateful to her.” Vlad currently attends Wildwood Elementary, where his mother also works as a para-educator. Vlad’s friends know he delivers the Piedmont Post, which he loves to mention on occasion. “Sometimes they say, ‘Oh, I want to do that, too,’” he giggled. “You just have to ask.” When he isn’t delivering papers, Vlad likes to eat ice cream in Piedmont Park and play his favorite sports – basketball and soccer and do martial arts. “Soccer is my favorite,” he remarked proudly. “My favorite position is to play striker.” Vlad thinks that if anyone else should have a paper route with the Post, it should be his best friend, Maxim, who also attends Wildwood Elementary. “He would be good at it. I think he would like to earn money.” For more information about getting a paper route with the Piedmont Post, please contact our office via phone at 652-2051 or via email at news@piedmont-post.com. New paperboy at the Piedmont Post Ukranian Vlad Putrenkov now delivering for the neighborhood By Matt Simons Ever y Wednesday after school, third-grader Vlad Putrenkov walks to the Piedmont Center for the Arts to pick up a stack of papers and tucks them into his canvas delivery bag. After folding his supply of papers, he delivers the Piedmont Post to subscribers on his route, which includes Highland, Requa and Wildwood Avenue. “The hardest part is carrying the bag,” said Putrenkov. “It gets to be around 15 pounds, once a month for the All-City edition.” After nearly three months on the job, Putrenkov can now land his papers squarely at front doors with startling accuracy. “It’s just like baseball,” he said. And Vlad loves baseball. Vlad began delivering in February 2024 when he was put in touch with the Piedmont Post by his mother’s friend, Mary Ann Parachini, who thought it would be a good way for him to meet members of the community. The son of Ukrainian immigrants Alexander Putrenkov and Maryna Putrenkova, Vlad and his family came to the United States in April 2022 following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian War just two months earlier. “It was scary,” recalled Maryna. “They were shooting. The city immediately closed schools, hospitals, and grocery stores were left without food. There were armed soldiers and tanks on the streets. The police ceased to exist, and thefts became more frequent. People were kidnapped.” Since moving to Piedmont with the help of a sponsorship from Piedmont Community Church, the Putrenkov family has adjusted well to the town. Maryna said the greatest surprise was the kindness of the community. “The Miller family took us in for a while and helped get Vlad into Wildwood School. They also introduced us to the church in Piedmont where we made many friends. We are very grateful to the Miller family and our church members for helping us adapt to this country at such a difficult time for us.” She also thanked Piedmont resident Mary Ann Parachini for allowing her family to stay at her house for a short period. “We are also very grateful to her.” Vlad currently attends Wildwood Elementary, where his mother also works as a para-educator. Vlad’s friends know he delivers the Piedmont Post, which he loves to mention on occasion. “Sometimes they say, ‘Oh, I want to do that, too,’” he giggled. “You just have to ask.” When he isn’t delivering papers, Vlad likes to eat ice cream in Piedmont Park and play his favorite sports – basketball and soccer and do martial arts. “Soccer is my favorite,” he remarked proudly. “My favorite position is to play striker.” Vlad thinks that if anyone else should have a paper route with the Post, it should be his best friend, Maxim, who also attends Wildwood Elementary. “He would be good at it. articles.text: Photos by Becky Spies Xander Schulte-Sasse closed his high school career at the NCS Meet of Champions. Piedmont’s track and field team concluded its season at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions at Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 17-18. The year’s team had a school-record 21 athletes qualify for the prestigious event. “When we started the season we weren’t sure what to expect, with 79 of our 109 athletes being freshmen and sophomores. Fast forward to the end of the championship run and we learned that we had the focus, will power, and character to push through,” noted PHS coach Pouyan Assadi “My final takeaway is that we’ll have giant shoes to fill with some very highly talented seniors graduating, but we have the depth and upside talent to take things to the next level over the next few year,” Assadi added. Closing a productive high school career in a big way was Xander Schulte-Sasse, who placed sixth of the 24 runners in the 3200 meters with a time of 9:21.90. It marks a strong close to his high school career and senior year after suffering an injury late in the cross-country season in the fall. “Xander missed three months of training from November to the start of track season, and he worked super hard to get here. Around lap-six, the field thinned out and we knew that as long as he held on tight he’d get on the podium,” Assadi said. It was also a strong performance from hurdler Ella Yasar. A junior, she reached the finals of the 300-meter hurdles on Saturday, finishing fifth of eight finalists with a time of 47.03. The previous day, Yasar was sixth of 22 athletes in the preliminary round, clocking a 47.22. “Simply put, Ella got it done. She capped off her monster season with back to back PRs and got on the podium to claim her first ever MOC medal. I can’t express enough what a privilege it is to be her coach. She deserves every moment and I loved seeing her smile ear to ear,” Assadi said. Girls Results Senior Breah Bell competed in two individual events. She placed 13th of 23 in the long jump with a distance of 16 feet, 8.25 inches, while she was 14th of 24 in the 100 meter dash preliminary round in 12.66. Bell also competed on the 4x100 relay team as the anchor leg. articles.text: Piedmont wins Spirit Award at Spaghetti Western Tournament Piedmont Middle School’s ultimate team, Purple Reign, wrapped up the competitive spring season with a second place finish in Bay Area Disc Association’s premier youth ultimate tournament, Spaghetti Western on May 4 in Stockton. Purple Reign’s Varsity squad (seeded 7th out of 10 teams) competed in the Middle School Division 1 of the tournament, when torrential rain and winds suspended the tournament midway through the day. This was only the second year that the team competed in Middle School Division 1 play. Purple Reign went 2-0 in pool play thanks to a stifling zone defense that created turnovers that the team was able to turn into goals. The team beat Baja Sunset (a team from Tijuana, Baja California) 8-7 and the Claremont Seawolves 6-3. The team featured superb handling by Aidan Stewart (7th grade), Ari Lopez (8th grade), and Drew DeVries (8th grade); strong defense by Ariel Grossberg (8th grade), Noah Hildebrand (8th grade), and Shane McNulty (8th grade); and leading scorer, Ben McMurtry (7th grade). Tournament bracket play was played at El Cerrito High School on Saturday, May 18th on a sunny day with winds gusts that tested players’ throwing and catching abilities. Purple Reign was victorious over Alameda Taurus 6-2 in the semifinals; but lost a close championship game to the Claremont Seawolves 6-7. The team was supported by reserves Ethan Grossberg (6th grade), Sawyer Heppner (6th grade) and Zach Fisher (6th grade). Purple Reign capped off a competitive day of ultimate by winning the Spirit Award. All youth ultimate tournaments feature a Spirit Award where teams rate each opposing team on their spirit and the team with the highest average spirit score wins the award. articles.text: Staff Photos Coach Jordan Seiden (left) talks things over with the football team following a spring practice session. Spring is a time when many high school football programs begin training and installing systems to prepare for the fall season. Last year Piedmont players were not on the field until the summertime. They had no home field due to renovation of Witter Field and with a squad of only 13 players. This time around, there’s no shortage of optimism after PHS won the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division title. It resulted in a varsity group of around 30 athletes reporting to training camp thus year, “We didn’t have spring ball last year. We had a small spring practice my first year. We’re about up to 30 today and 5-6 significant players aren’t here yet. We have some new faces,” coach Jordan Seiden said following practice on Monday this week. Junior Sam Shelby, entering his third varsity year, has watched the development of the Sam Shelby reels in a reception during spring practice team under Seiden. “Last year, we learned a lot and improved as a team; it showed on the field, for sure. This year, we can take all that knowledge and apply it on the field. You can see the differences between this year and previous years in how much we’re learning as a team, I think it’ll make a big difference this year,” Shelby said. There is a different vibe around the Piedmont High football team. It’s no-longer a team looking to revitalize itself as when Seiden took over in 2022. Instead it is a team looking to continue building its culture and lift more championship banners next fall. “It’s crazy to see. It all happened so fast to me. All the guys show up every day and put in the work on and off the field. It comes naturally now,” Shelby said. Piedmont captured last year’s Shoreline title by defeating Newark Memorial in a heated 29-26 victory on the road. It was the team’s first league championship since 2015. Next season, PHS and Newark will compete in the more difficult WACC Mission Division. In 2023, the Highlanders were forced to play the entire season on the road due to continued delays of the renovations at Witter Field. PHS will be back under the Friday Night Lights of Witter in 2024. “It’s great to see. We were wondering all winter about how many kids would come back. The optimism was high based off of last year’s progress. It’s a real football culture now, we had great support from parents who really understood the vision we had,” Seiden said. Shelby, a receiver and defensive back, finished last year’s season with several honors. He was the SF Chronicle’s Player of the Year for the East Bay region, was named to the Chronicle’s All-Metro first-team, the Mercury News’ All-Bay Area second team, and was the Shoreline Division’s Player of the Year. Shelby competed on the track team this spring but suffered a season-ending injury. He’s back at full strength in football practice and is looking to move past the track season. “It’s tough because I’m a competitive guy and I still had that itch when I got hurt. Track is a big part of recruiting for football too, so that kind of slowed things down. But we’re back now and I just have to put it behind me,” Shelby said. The Highlanders look ahead

The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team, which includes high school club racing and a junior development middle school team, competed in its final races over two weekends at Six Sigma Winery, a private ranch in Lower Lake. They recently raced the NICA NorCal League Championship on Sunday, May 19, while they also raced at Six Sigma the previous week on Saturday, May 11. Six Sigma Winery includes rolling and rocky terrain through oak trees around a meadow where teams camped. The high school course lap for varsity riders was 16 miles with 2,000 feet of elevation gain, the JV 1 race was 12 miles with 1,500 feet of elevation gain, while the JV 2 event was eight miles with 1,000 feet of vertical gain. NICA NorCal Championship In the Varsity Boys race, graduating seniors Max Rivera was 38th of 63 riders with a time of 1:42:05. Matteo Scanu placed 40th in 1:43:14, Schuyler Sawicki was 43rd in 1:44:02, and Mark Hsia finished 47th in 1:45:33. articles.text: PBSF names “Livin’ The Dream” award winners The Dragons of the Piedmont Softball Foundation won the East Bay Pony Premier League on May 16. Pictured are (front) Robby Koch (left), Abe Mandel, John Arney, Drew DeVries, Ari Moskovitz, Russell Pan; (back) Coach Steve Long, Cyrus Emanuelson, Chase Knapp, Sean Heafey, Mateo Long, Alex Mikhailov, and Head Coach Danilo Juarez. The Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation Dragons emerged triumphant as champions of the 2024 East Bay Pony Premier League (EBPPL). Comprising ten formidable 14U teams from the cities of Piedmont, Orinda, Moraga, and Lafayette, the EBPPL had d intense competition throughout the season. The Dragons, with an impressive regular-season record of 11-3-1, secured the top seed in the post-season tournament. Their dominance continued into the playoffs, where they swept four consecutive victories. In a high-stakes showdown on Thursday, May 16, the Dragons faced the third-seeded Lafayette Pink Bombers at Humphries Diamond. The Dragons executed near-perfection, shutting out their opponents with a resounding 9-0 victory. The pitching trio of Cyrus Emanuelson, Drew DeVries, and Robby Koch combined forces to no-hit the Bombers. Their stellar performance was complemented by outstanding defensive plays from Robby Koch, Abe Mandel, Mateo Long, and Russell Pan. Alex Mikhailov, behind the plate, thwarted base runners and allowed only one stolen base, while the Dragons swiped ten bases themselves. Offensively, Mateo Long, Cyrus Emanuelson, and Ari Moskovitz each notched two base hits. Long’s lead-off double in the fourth inning set the tone, and Emanuelson drove in three crucial runs. John Arney’s line-drive RBI single in the fifth inning ignited a five-run surge, breaking open the game. The championship clash on Sunday, May 19th, pitted the Dragons against the Piedmont Spartans. The Dragons wasted no time, erupting for six runs in the opening frame. Consecutive base hits by Long, Pan, Emanuelson, and Mikhailov fueled the offensive onslaught. Chase Knapp drove in a run and scored on Sean Heafy’s clutch two-out RBI double to add to the tally, securing a commanding lead. Heafey finished the day with three RBIs. Pan, Emanuelson, Mikhailov, and DeVries all contributed with two base hits. The combined efforts of Cyrus Emanuelson, Abe Mandel, and Drew Devries on the mound resulted in a four-hit shutout, sealing the Dragons’ championship triumph. The PBSF Dragons have etched their names in baseball lore, celebrating a well-deserved victory in the heart of East Bay baseball. Murray played youth baseball with Hall of Famer Robin Yount, and while Murray didn’t have the same skills of the future hall of famer, Murray was fond of telling anyone that his love of the game helped Yount fulfill his achievements in baseball. Former PBSF Board member Barry Barnes said, “Every time I asked, ‘how are you doing, Murray?’ His response was almost always, ‘I’m living the dream man, living the dream.’” Murray carried the positive attitude from youth baseball throughout his life. After his passing in late 2012, PBSF created the “Livin’ the Dream” award in his honor. The “Livin’ the Dream” award is given to one player on each team. The award is not a MVP award, but rather it is given to a player who embodies positive, intangible contributions to the team, sportsmanship, perseverance, and a positive infectious attitude like Murray Davis. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s summer season opens on May 30 with Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas the composer completed before his death in 1791. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920’s Berlin cabaret. Kim, who conducted The Magic Flute with multiple European companies as well as with the Washington National Opera, will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation of the opera in nearly a decade. The cast includes New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, nine performances of The Magic Flute are scheduled between May 30 and June 26. To purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s newest production, Head Over Heels, premieres this Saturday, May 25. Head Over Heels is based on a book of the same name by Jeff Whitty, and adapted for the stage by James Magruder. The play mixes pop punk and poetic prose as it explores a royal family’s narrative of love, friendship, gender, and sexuality to the tunes of the 1980’s all-female rock band The Go-Go’s. “I am really excited to delve into the theme of self-acceptance that Head Over Heels highlights,” said Director Mel Martinez. “To speak your truth is scary, but when you are truly yourself, everything looks better – even tastes better! It’s like being in love. I also love these characters to bits. This beautiful adventure they go on helps them break the molds society is comfortable with, and I find that inspiring.” Head Over Heels will be performed on the Berkeley Playhouse stage through June 30. articles.text: An exhibition featuring the work of widely-recognized photographer Irving Penn is on view at the de Young Museum in San Francisco through July 21. Penn is Vogue Magazine’s longest-standing contributor, and he has become the most influential fashion photographer in the postwar era. Known for his use of neutral backgrounds, Penn emphasized models’ personalities through their gestures and expressions. The exhibition includes 175 photographs, spanning every period of Penn’s nearly 70-year career and ranging from early documentary scenes, celebrity portraits and workers with the tools of their trades to abstract nudes and fashion studies. This presentation also features a special section of photographs made during Penn’s 1967 trip to San Francisco, where he captured scenes from the iconic “Summer of Love.” Included are his portraits of hippies, members of the Hells Angels Motorcycle Club and local rock bands the Grateful Dead and Big Brother and the Holding Company. On Saturday, May 30, the exhibit’s co-curator Jeff Rosenheim will share various stories on pieces being shown and what transpired behind-the-scenes in making this exhibition. The lecture is free and begins at 2:30 p.m. in the museum’s Koret Auditorium To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ irving-penn?mc_cid=20ab0f- 52d7&mc_eid=573801a180. pages.text: Wednesday, May 22, 2024 17 Head Over Heels premieres Sat. at Berkeley Playhouse By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Playhouse’s newest production, Head Over Heels, premieres this Saturday, May 25. Head Over Heels is based on a book of the same name by Jeff Whitty, and adapted for the stage by James Magruder. The play mixes pop punk and poetic prose as it explores a royal family’s narrative of love, friendship, gender, and sexuality to the tunes of the 1980’s all-female rock band The Go-Go’s. “I am really excited to delve into the theme of self-acceptance that Head Over Heels highlights,” said Director Mel Martinez. “To speak your truth is scary, but when you are truly yourself, everything looks better – even tastes better! It’s like being in love. I also love these characters to bits. This beautiful adventure they go on helps them break the molds society is comfortable with, and I find that inspiring.” Head Over Heels will be performed on the Berkeley Playhouse stage through June 30. To purchase tickets, visit https:// tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/. articles.text: Annual event has florists interpreting classic art with flowers Opening night during Bouquets to Art in 2023 at the de Young Museum. The de Young Museum will be holding its annual floral exhibition Bouquets to Art from June 4 to June 9. Celebrating its 40th anniversary this year, Bouquets to Art allows museumgoers to engage with the de Young’s expansive collections in a novel way – with floral interpretations of some of the museum’s classic art. For one week only, the leading floral designers of the Bay Area will return to the galleries this summer to showcase their creative botanical arrangements inspired by museum masterworks. From sculptures to sketches, nothing remains off-limits as a source of inspiration. Florists will then display their works in front of the various paintings, woodcarvings and other pieces for audiences to see. Photo by Drew Altizer Photo by Drew Altizer Kirk Wilder and Jeremiah Allen reinterpret Berkeley #3 (1953) by Richard Diebenkorn for Bouquets to Art 2023. Photo by Drew. Altizer Pico Soriano reinterprets A Taste of Gumbo (1990) by Robert Colescott for Bouquets to Art 2023. Photo by Valerie Lee Valerie Lee of J. Miller Flowers reinterpreted The Wild Swan (1900) by Alexander Pope for a previous year’s Bouquets to Art. This year’s exhibit marks the 25th year that Valerie Lee of J. Miller Flowers has participated. In previous years, Lee has interpreted paintings of dresses, sunsets and swans as striking, vibrant flower arrangements. This year, she will have a floral piece based upon the museum’s collection of New Guinean ceremonial shields. Lee said that the most difficult part of the exhibition has always been keeping the flower fresh between showings. “That’s the challenge of participating in this. You want to make sure every museumgoer has a chance to see the same, refreshing flowers,” she said. The exhibit will also feature a raffle of fresh arrangements from the museum’s flower cart, and eventgoers are encouraged to take part in engaging lectures with renowned designers and authors happening throughout the week. Opening night is Monday, June 4, at 5:30 p.m. Complimentary parking in the Music Concourse Parking Garage is provided for all guests. Food and drinks will be prepared and served by McCalls Catering & Events. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Dr in San Francisco. Tickets can be purchased online at www. famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Advance tickets are required for this event.

articles.text: Denzel Washington and Viola Davis have offered to filmgoers not only a master class in acting, but Washington, as director and actor, has created a startlingly fine film adaptation of August Wilson’s 1983 Pulitzer Prize-winning play, Fences. For the actors, it’s a tour de force bringing to bear their immense talent. They are remarkable in their ability to so completely inhabit the characters – Washington as Troy Maxson, a 53-year-old trash collector who carries with him a stone of embitterment, and Davis as his wife, Rose, who has invested 18 years of her life standing besides him, shoulder to shoulder, all while remaining undaunted. The place is Pittsburg. The year is 1957. The setting, in great part, is the backyard of the Maxon’s hard-used brick row house. It’s summer, and it’s there in that enclosed space, that Troy and his friend and fellow trash collector Bono (Stephen Henderson), return each day after work. While sipping gin, they reflect on life as they know it to be. Troy, once a gifted baseball player in the Negro league, laments the color barrier that kept him from breaking into the majors. He insists – reaching down into a well of anger and regret – that his color kept him from fulfilling a dream that was all but within his grasp. Jackie Robinson shattered that ceiling of bigotry in 1947, but it was too late for Troy. Denzel Washington and Viola Davis in Fences Rose has heard this story for years and futilely points out to her husband that it wasn’t ever meant to be because history and his age betrayed him; now his life is what it is. That racial and personal intersection that haunts Troy frames his life and follows him like a dark, bitter shadow. He had the right stuff, he says, defiantly. He brought the heat, better than all those white boys in the majors ever dreamed of doing. August Wilson’s gift is not only his ability to create a time and place, but he also relies on language for texture, meaning authentic dialogue that is colloquial and powerful and true. Wilson, through Troy and Rose, burrows deep into his characters and their lives, both noble and flawed, always tinged with regret, even in their best moments. With Troy, his sentences are filled with provocation and power, are always dense with meaning and rhythm — often reliant on baseball metaphors. Rose is his counterweight: softer, wiser, yet steely in her understanding of this man she so deeply loves. Troy’s 18-year-old son, Cory (Jovan Adepo), has far less insight into his father, so their encounters are often a battle of wills and hardheaded confrontations. It is Washington’s intention to produce/direct what is referred to as Wilson’s 10-play cycle, each capturing an aspect of the African-American experience. Fences is the first. The film, in every way, pays homage to a gifted writer who created a panoply of stories and characters that capture the human condition in all its pain and tenacity from a point of view not often revealed or understood for reasons that are both historical and cultural. Fences is extraordinary. Fences. Directed by Denzel Washington. Starring Denzel Washington, Viola Davis, Stephen Henderson. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2016. Now streaming on prime/Fandango/Paramount+. tv

With his years of experience, Henry is not an easy kill and so he grabs Danny, calls a friend, and they fly south to Cartagena, Colombia, where it’s assumed they can vanish. For reasons still a mystery, the bad guys find them. And so begins act two, which is when the story falls off the rails and in just a few scenes goes from a solid enough plot to that familiar geography known as suspend your disbelief. Apparently, the three-letter agency this time sends not a team of paramilitary types, but just one exceptionally skilled killer who is Henry’s doppelganger, only a lot younger. A fact that Danny immediately notices. Who the killer is and why he is sent to take out Henry involves a Gemini black ops project director Clay Verris (Clive Owen), a previous mentor of Henry’s. Suddenly DNA and cloning are involved, taking the story into the realm of sci-fi/fantasy, which only slows down what was, until then, a pretty good story that didn’t need a surreal plot detour. There are two questions begged: what’s a multi Oscar winner like Ang Lee (Brokeback Mountain, Life of Pi) doing at the helm of a poorly written, pulpy B-movie like “Gemini Man”? Was it the new de-aging film technology when applied to Smith allows him to play both roles (aging retiree and young wannabe hit man)? Or was it the opportunity to shoot the film in an accelerated frame format (120 frames per second as opposed to the standard 24 frames per second), which allows the colors to really pop. Cartagena is shown in vivid pastels, the narrow street buildings all but glowing and gorgeous. There is one scene where a sky blue jeep drives along a raised highway and all but demands that the audience not take their eyes off what is less than an extraordinary car. It was the contextual color that created a can’t look away moment. In thinking back on the look of the film, I never found the 120 frames a distraction; rather there were moments that were incandescent. The thing is that it was Ang Lee’s rep as a superb filmmaker that caused me to watch Gemini Man and not to forget the proven charm of Will Smith whose characters are usually saturated with an insouciance style. But neither Lee, nor Smith, nor Winstead can save this film from its failure of imagination. Gemini Man. Directed by Ang Lee. Starring Will Smith, Mary Elizabeth Winstead, Clive Owen. 1 hr., 57 min. articles.text: Chris Honoré The BFG is a remarkable animated story, directed by Steven Spielberg, steeped in wondrous characters and gentle goodwill. With one exception, and it’s that exception that gives me pause when suggesting this feature film. All things considered, it may be best suited for youngsters on the cusp of tweenhood. But more about that later. The narrative, based on the popular Roald Dahl 1982 novel of the same name, begins with 8-year-old Sophie who lives in a Dickensian orphanage. Unable to sleep, she often roams the dark hallways, or often stands looking out her bedroom window, staring down at the shadowed streets of London. On one such night, during the witching hour, she sees an extraordinary sight: a giant, carrying a suitcase and a trumpet, walking on the sidewalk below. We come to understand that his mission is blowing dreams through the opened windows of children while they sleep. Sophie, mesmerized by this enormous figure, unexpectedly locks eyes with the giant. Frightened, she turns and runs back to the safety of her bed (or so she believes). However, the giant, worried that Sophie might disclose his presence, reaches through the window into her bedroom, and scoops her up, deciding to take her back to Giant Land. Sophie is breathtakingly afraid. Of course, she’s heard the A scene from The BFG tales about how giants not only capture children, but they regard them as tasty morsels. However this giant, when Sophie tells him why she is terrified, laughs. He explains that he is a BFG, a big friendly giant, and all he ever eats are snozzcumbers (like cucumbers) and only drinks frobscotties, a fizzy drink that causes loud flatulence, called whizzpoppers. Soon Sophie and BFG, despite their initial bickering, form a bond of mutual friendship. The neighborhood giants, much bigger than BFG, who is 24 feet tall, bully him, much to the consternation of Sophie. Naturally, when they come around she is told to hide. These massive, lumbering creatures are, after all, a rough crowd with strange, creepy names, like Fleshlumpeater and Bloodbottler. But then, as Sophie soon discovers, giants speak a very different language, a patois of sorts, mixed up but interesting. Sophie is precocious and therefore able to convince BFG that something must be done about these mean, rogue giants. She insists that they go to London and speak with Queen Elizabeth (Penelope Wilton) about the threat the giants pose to the children. And thus, Sophie’s adventure continues. Older kids will be captivated by this classic, wonderfully animated tale. But then there is something about giants that is impossibly compelling. The BFG. Directed by Steven Spielberg. With his years of experience, Henry is not an easy kill and so he grabs Danny, calls a friend, and they fly south to Cartagena, Colombia, where it’s assumed they can vanish. For reasons still a mystery, the bad guys find them. And so begins act two, which is when the story falls off the rails and in just a few scenes goes from a solid enough plot to that familiar geography known as suspend your disbelief. Apparently, the three-letter agency this time sends not a team of paramilitary types, but just one exceptionally skilled killer who is Henry’s doppelganger, only a lot younger. A fact that Danny immediately notices. Who the killer is and why he is sent to take out Henry involves a Gemini black ops project director Clay Verris (Clive Owen), a previous mentor of Henry’s. Suddenly DNA and cloning are involved, taking the story into the realm of sci-fi/fantasy, which only slows down what was, until then, a pretty good story that didn’t need a surreal plot detour. There are two questions begged: what’s a multi Oscar winner like Ang Lee (Brokeback Mountain, Life of Pi) doing at the helm of a poorly written, pulpy B-movie like “Gemini Man”? Was it the new de-aging film technology when applied to Smith allows him to play both roles (aging retiree and young wannabe hit man)? Or was it the opportunity to shoot the film in an accelerated frame format (120 frames per second as opposed to the standard 24 frames per second), which allows the colors to really pop. Cartagena is shown in vivid pastels, the narrow street buildings all but glowing and gorgeous. There is one scene where a sky blue jeep drives along a raised highway and all but demands that the audience not take their eyes off what is less than an extraordinary car. It was the contextual color that created a can’t look away moment. In thinking back on the look of the film, I never found the 120 frames a distraction; rather there were moments that were incandescent. The thing is that it was Ang Lee’s rep as a superb filmmaker that caused me to watch Gemini Man and not to forget the proven charm of Will Smith whose characters are usually saturated with an insouciance style. But neither Lee, nor Smith, nor Winstead can save this film from its failure of imagination. Gemini Man. Directed by Ang Lee. Starring Will Smith, Mary Elizabeth Winstead, Clive Owen. 1 hr., 57 min. articles.text: Marilynn Hodgson, a longtime Piedmont resident, died peacefully the morning of May 11, 2024, just a few weeks shy of her 94th birthday, following several years battling dementia. Marilynn led a long, rich and fulfilling life. Born Marilynn Louise Davis in Grand Rapids, Michigan, she was the only daughter of Dr. David and Lilith Davis. She was raised in Grand Rapids until the outbreak of World War II. After Pearl Harbor, Dr. Davis enlisted and became the Chief of Psychiatry for the First Air Force, whose mission was the defense of the Northeast and Great Lakes regions of the United States. They moved about the East Coast until the end of the war, returning to East Grand Rapids, with Marilynn graduating from East Grand Rapids High School in 1948. Marilynn attended the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor (Go Blue) and graduated in 1952 with a BA in English and a minor in Art History. She was a member of Kappa Delta sorority and remained lifelong friends with sorority sister Peg Carter. In the Summer after her graduation, she traveled with three fellow Michigan alumni to Europe. From that point on, she was hooked on travel. Forever attracted to fashion and high society, in 1953 she attended the Tobé-Coburn School for Fashion Careers in New York City, aiming for a career in merchandising. She worked for a spell at J.L. Hudson (Hudson’s) department store in Detroit, Michigan. A visit to San Francisco to see her uncle, U.S. Army Colonel Carl Lundquist, the Commanding Officer at the Presidio of San Francisco his wife Thelma would forever change her life. She loved San Francisco and the Golden State on the spot. As I look back over the years of those tastings, there is one other winery that deserved a place in the Zinfandel pantheon. It has appeared in my top ten list year after year – Robert Biale. Robert Biale Winery remains what has it has always been – a small family owned and run winery that cares passionately about Zinfandel (and Petite Sirah). In 1937, four years after the repeal of prohibition, Pietro Biale, Robert’s grandfather, planted Zinfandel vines among all his other produce Robert Biale Winery 4038 Big Ranch Rd. Napa, CA 94558 (707) 257-7555 on his ranch in Napa Valley. The farm grew walnuts, prunes, other fruits and vegetables and also functioned as a chicken ranch. Pietro’s son Aldo expanded the production of Zinfandel which he sold “on the down low” to friends and neighbors to avoid government regulation. In 1991, Aldo’s son Robert Biale and a small group of friends established the Robert Biale Winery. The winery has now grown to produce about 15,000 cases annually and an amazing 30 different wines. I had the pleasure to visit Robert Biale Winery recently and winemaker David Natali poured some of the winery’s current releases. • 2023 Clementina Greco Bianco This is the only white wine Biale makes. An obscure Italian varietal, the Greco Bianco has a beautiful citrus nose with a touch of honeysuckle. On the palate, it is bursting with grapefruit and melon fruit flavors and has great acidity and balance. A perfect aperitif on a warm afternoon. • 2023 Rosato This rose is made from Sangiovese grapes. Aromas of strawberries jump from the glass. The body of the wine is light in the Provencal style with cherry fruit flavors and a clean dry finish. • 2021 Black Chicken Zinfandel This is sort of the flagship wine for Biale and is a blend of several different vineyards. It rolls effortlessly out of the glass with enticing scents of raspberries, raisins, and plums with nuances of cinnamon, cloves and earth. Medium-bodied and spicy in the mouth, it has soft tannins and refreshing acidity finishing on a lingering peppery note. • 2021 R.W. Moore Zinfandel This has often been my favorite of the Biale Zinfandels. It has dense aromas of blackberries, licorice, violets and leather, gaining more nuance with time in the glass. The palate is full-bodied and deeply fruited, with a firm and fresh frame and long, layered finish. The nose is delicate and pretty with scents of raspberry jam, apricots and citrus peel. The palate is medium to light-bodied, soft, bright and approachable with a floral character lingering on the finish. • 2021 Pagani Ranch Zinfandel This historic old vineyard is a field blend with lots of Alicante Bouchet, Carignan and who knows what else thrown into the mix. It opens with wild tones of earth, tar and graphite that give way to wild blackberries and currant hints. The palate is impressive, intensely fruited, silky and fresh. articles.text: When you’re creating your estate plan, your biggest priority may be taking care of your family – your spouse, grown children, grandchildren, and other loved ones. And as you think of where you want your assets to go, you also may be thinking about how to be fair – but is that the same as treating everyone equally? In estate planning, “equal” doesn’t always mean “fair.” Let’s consider some factors that can help explain the difference: • Need – It’s highly unlikely that the individuals you want to include in your estate plan — especially your adult children – have the same family and financial situations. For example, you could have one child who is extremely successful and has no children of their own, while another child earns much less income and supports three children. Clearly, your two adult children have vastly different financial needs — so, you need to consider whether you want to treat them equally or fairly. If you decide you want to treat them fairly, you may want to divide your assets in a way that provides more help to the child who needs it most. • Abilities – You may well have some assets that you believe are more suitable for one child over another. This can be especially true if you are planning on passing on a family business. If you know that one child is the most capable of running the business or has been primarily involved in the business, then you may want to give that child control as a next-generation owner. Yet, this may not seem fair to another child, who might also express interest in the business, so you may want to look for ways to provide this child with enough assets to help make the overall inheritance more equal • Practicality – In some instances, you might think you can meet both the “fair” and “equal” criteria. Suppose, for instance, that you have a cabin or other vacation home that you think two of your children could share. In theory, this joint ownership might sound good, but in practical terms, it could cause problems. Are both children equally willing and capable of paying taxes and upkeep on the cabin or vacation home? What if one child wants to sell their share? And then, there’s the question of who gets to use the property at various times of the year. All these issues should be resolvable, but they can also cause great stress within the family. There’s no simple formula for solving the fair-versus-equal dilemma. But keep this in mind: Communicating your wishes to your loved ones while you are drawing up your estate plan can help reduce confusion — and hopefully lead to fewer hard feelings — when you are no longer around. By their nature, fairness and equality issues related to estate plans can trigger a range of emotions, and addressing these feelings beforehand can help provide a great service for your loved ones. You might also find that some objectivity can be valuable. That’s why, when creating your estate plan, you may benefit by working with a team of professionals, including your legal, financial and tax advisors. When developing your estate plan, you might well strive for equality and fairness but above all, you want to get things right. And careful planning, open communication and appropriate guidance can help go a long way toward this goal. articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson In my early 20s, less than a year out of college, I got addicted to berries. Until then I’d only eaten berries from the grocery store. But then I went to work at the Bainbridge Island Review, a twiceweekly community newspaper near Seattle, and was asked to profile a local strawberry farmer. He gave me a funny-looking, pinkish strawberry. I took a bite. Juice drizzled down the front of my shirt and ruined it forever. And the flavor! It was like having a Vosges truffle when all I’d known was Hershey’s kisses. You never find these local varieties in grocery stores. They can only last a day or two on the shelf before melting into goo. But the juiciness and sweetness hooked me forever. When the Pacific Northwest rains abated and I started riding my bicycle to work, I noticed an enormous blackberry bramble along the edge of a vacant lot. Every morning I’d stop, pick a half pint of berries, and eat them at my desk for breakfast. I plucked only those that were the softest, most sun-ripened, and most delicious. Years later, reading the book Jamberry to my young kids brought back memories of Bainbraidge Berryland and inspired me to re-create it at home. My taste buds were not the Once a staple of Native Americans, thimbleberries taste great but produce very little fruit. Raspberries fruit for most of the year, but the best season is spring. only motivators. I needed to grow something on my front yard’s split-rail fence to keep out loose dogs and kids. What could be better than a thorny berry bramble? After cultivating multiple varieties over the course of a decade, I strongly suggest you try the marionberry. Hailing from Marion County, Oregon, it’s the world’s most widely cultivated blackberry variety. Allowing the fruits to ripen on the vine before you harvest them will really set them apart from the ones you find in stores. Cultivating blackberries requires a lot of pruning. Left to their own devices, the vines will take over everything. I prune mine back severely in the fall, mostly give them free rein in the spring – lest I prune off a bunch of ripening berries – and then prune them regularly all summer. My raspberry patch has also fared quite well – perhaps too well. Lacking thorns and growing more upright than blackberries, raspberries share their cousins’ tendency to take over everything. I follow a similar pruning strategy as with blackberries, but raspberries can be harder to deal with as they will fruit almost year-round at the very tip of each shoot. My kids, who visit the raspberry patch almost daily, always complain when my pruning efforts lop off unripe berry clusters. Ripening loganberries Can’t decide between blackberries and raspberries? Try the loganberry. A cross between a North American blackberry and European raspberry, it makes plump fruits with a slightly reddish hue that taste amazing. This is hands-down my favorite berry. I haven’t had as much luck growing strawberries, though I’ve tried. They too often got eaten by squirrels or insects. If you want to cultivate something that you won’t find even at a farmer’s market, consider the native thimbleberry. Once a staple for Native Americans, thimbleberries grow across the West and Upper Midwest, though they are particularly dominant as an understory plant in the Pacific Northwest. Their delicious red fruits taste like stronger, less juicy versions of raspberries. Compared to most other berries, thimbleberries take well to shade but also produce much less fruit – typically only a handful of berries per plant. That’s probably why nobody sells them commercially. Not everything with value can turn a profit. That’s one thing that certain kinds of berries and certain forms of journalism have in common! Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. A split-rail fence is a great place for a berry bramble.

Among those participating were: Bill Ahern, Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Brenda Ferrero, Lois Price, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Lee Hambrick, Priscilla Wanerus, Joyce Ahern, Jim Kellogg, Lori Austin, Alicia Rivera, Mark Davis, Bob Wong, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Linda Peacock, Peggy Schultz, Tina Shum, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Martin Levy, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Janet and Mark Laurent, Quincy Dong, Nava Shaham, Elizabeth Richter, Irene Thompson, Sherry Jacobs, Claudine Bach, Lisa Euphrat, Sarah Johnson, Ken Moy, Pat Nichols and Rick Eigenbrode, Alissa Quan, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Maci Negron, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Daksha Talati who was walking with them for the first time. There was big turnout of 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays walk. Each year the Piedmont Planning Commission recognizes a small number of outstanding construction projects in Piedmont with Design Awards. They reflect the highest level of design excellence among all those that have come before the commission during the prior year. Three walkers, Eric Behrens, Mike Henn, and Jim Kellogg, are former planning commissioners. They said the selection process is for city staff to nominate their favorite projects and for the commissioners to pick the winners. This year the commission also introduced Sustainability Awards to celebrate property owners who have incorporated green elements like heat pumps, solar panels, and greywater systems into their homes. Seven projects were selected for 2024 Design Awards that span a range of project types. The walkers wanted to see the winners, and realized they could get to five of them in a 2.5-mile loop. The first was at 218 Bonita Avenue, Anna Putnam and Daniel Rampton’s winner of the Outstanding Integrated Addition award. Initially, the walkers couldn’t tell where the addition was due to a seamlessly-built extension to the original house. Only newer looking windows provided a clue. The next award winner was a bit of a hike, across town to Nace Avenue near Beach School. Stephen Selkowitz and Barbara O’Hare’s winner of the Excellence in Integrated Garage Design is at 22 Nace. The garage is a well-made, small replica of the home. Continuing on, they went to 11 Cambridge Way, the home of Peter Jaeschke and Supina Mapon, winner of the Excellence in Facade Composition Award. The new covered front porch with two white columns provide a dramatic new entrance. The walkers went over to 337 Magnolia Avenue, winner of the Outstanding Architectural Restoration award. Owners Lukas Bruggemann and Wendi Sue have done a great job creating a lovely “new” home, with one of only two magnolia trees on Magnolia Avenue. Then it was up to 319 El Cerrito, the home of Gina Song and David Woo and winner of the Excellence in Garage to ADU Conversion award with a new, large unit that complemented this beautiful home that was built in 1921. That did the morning’s tour. The group returned to Magnolia Avenue and finished their walk back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. By Dick Carter There was big turnout of 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays walk. Each year the Piedmont Planning Commission recognizes a small number of outstanding construction projects in Piedmont with Design Awards. They reflect the highest level of design excellence among all those that have come before the commission during the prior year. Three walkers, Eric Behrens, Mike Henn, and Jim Kellogg, are former planning commissioners. They said the selection process is for city staff to nominate their favorite projects and for the commissioners to pick the winners. This year the commission also introduced Sustainability Awards to celebrate property owners who have incorporated green elements like heat pumps, solar panels, and greywater systems into their homes. Seven projects were selected for 2024 Design Awards that span a range of project types. The walkers wanted to see the winners, and realized they could get to five of them in a 2.5-mile loop. The first was at 218 Bonita Avenue, Anna Putnam and Daniel Rampton’s winner of the Outstanding Integrated Addition award. Initially, the walkers couldn’t tell where the addition was due to a seamlessly-built extension to the original house. Only newer looking windows provided a clue. The next award winner was a bit of a hike, across town to Nace Avenue near Beach School. Stephen Selkowitz and Barbara O’Hare’s winner of the Excellence in Integrated Garage Design is at 22 Nace. The garage is a well-made, small replica of the home. Continuing on, they went to 11 Cambridge Way, the home of Peter Jaeschke and Supina Mapon, winner of the Excellence in Facade Composition Award. The new covered front porch with two white columns provide a dramatic new entrance. The walkers went over to 337 Magnolia Avenue, winner of the Outstanding Architectural Restoration award. Owners Lukas Bruggemann and Wendi Sue have done a great job creating a lovely “new” home, with one of only two magnolia trees on Magnolia Avenue. Then it was up to 319 El Cerrito, the home of Gina Song and David Woo and winner of the Excellence in Garage to ADU Conversion award with a new, large unit that complemented this beautiful home that was built in 1921. That did the morning’s tour. The group returned to Magnolia Avenue and finished their walk back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge.
